    Preference tuning: DPO and ORPO

    After this lesson you can explain what preference data looks like, the intuition behind DPO's chosen-over-rejected objective, how ORPO combines SFT and preference in one stage, which member of the DPO family fits your data, how to read the rewards/* curves, and when preference tuning helps over plain SFT.

    Level: advanced Read time: ~16 min Prerequisites: Knowledge distillation III: did it work? Quality retained Verified: 13 Nov 2026

    SFT optimizes for one right answer per prompt. But many qualities you want — helpfulness, tone, safety, conciseness — aren't a single correct string; they're a preference between candidate responses. Preference tuning optimizes that directly.

    Preference data: chosen vs rejected

    Instead of (prompt → completion), preference data is (prompt → chosen, rejected): two responses to the same prompt, with a human (or a judge) saying which is better.

    { "prompt":   "Explain why the sky is blue to a five-year-old.",
  "chosen":   "The sky looks blue because sunlight is made of colors, and the air...",
  "rejected": "Rayleigh scattering causes shorter wavelengths to scatter more..." }

    Neither response is "wrong" — but for the audience, one is clearly better. SFT can't express that; preference tuning is built for it.

    DPO: optimize the preference directly

    Classic RLHF (Ouyang et al. 2022, arXiv 2203.02155) trained a separate reward model and then optimized against it with reinforcement learning — powerful but fiddly (Track 1's objectives lesson). Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al. 2023, arXiv 2305.18290) skips the reward model: it derives a loss directly from the (chosen, rejected) pairs that increases the model's relative likelihood of the chosen response over the rejected one. It uses a frozen copy of the starting model — the reference model — as an anchor, so the policy improves preferences without drifting arbitrarily far from where it started.

    # BrewSLM recipe "DPO Fast Start" (recipe.alignment.dpo.fast), main keys
training_mode: dpo
alignment_beta: 0.1        # DPO's β: higher = held closer to the reference
learning_rate: 1e-5
use_lora: true
num_epochs: 2
# required row fields: prompt, chosen, rejected

    β (alignment_beta) sets how strongly DPO is held to the reference model. It scales the implicit KL penalty: the DPO optimum is π* ∝ π_ref · exp(r/β) (Rafailov et al. 2023), and TRL's own docs say "higher β means less deviation from the reference model". So a higher β (e.g. 0.5) means smaller, safer moves; a lower β (e.g. 0.01–0.05) lets the policy move further from the reference, which shows an effect sooner but is easier to over-optimize. 0.1 is the common default (TRL's and BrewSLM's): a starting point, not a tuned value.

    ORPO: preference in a single stage

    The usual pipeline is two stages: SFT first, then DPO. ORPO (Odds Ratio Preference Optimization) (Hong et al. 2024, arXiv 2403.07691) folds them into one — it adds a preference term to the SFT loss, so a single training run both teaches the task and aligns to preferences, without a separate reference model or a separate SFT stage. Simpler pipeline, one pass over the data.

    BrewSLM's "ORPO Safe Start" recipe (recipe.alignment.orpo.safe) reuses the same alignment_beta key, but for ORPO it means something else: TRL reads it as ORPO's λ, the weight on the odds-ratio preference term relative to the SFT loss — not a pull toward a reference model, since ORPO has none.

    ORPO was designed to start from a base model: the SFT term teaches the task while the odds-ratio term pushes away from rejected answers, all in one run. Running ORPO on top of an SFT checkpoint works, but then you have two stages again and lose its main selling point. A larger λ puts more weight on the preference term relative to the SFT term.

    The DPO family

    DPO started a family of offline preference losses. They share the data shape (or relax it) and differ in what they optimize. You will see these names in papers and in TRL's options:

    MethodWhat changesReach for it whenIn TRL 1.x
    DPO (Rafailov et al. 2023, arXiv 2305.18290)Sigmoid loss on the β-scaled log-ratio gap between chosen and rejected, against a frozen reference.The default for paired data on top of an SFT model.DPOConfig(loss_type=["sigmoid"]) (default)
    IPO (Azar et al. 2023, arXiv 2310.12036)A squared loss that targets a fixed margin instead of pushing it ever wider, so it doesn't overfit pairs where one answer always wins.Near-deterministic preferences, or DPO that keeps over-optimizing.loss_type=["ipo"]; β is IPO's τ
    KTO (Ethayarajh et al. 2024, arXiv 2402.01306)Works on unpaired data: each row is one answer labelled good or bad.You have thumbs-up / thumbs-down feedback, not pairs (see Lesson 4.11's feedback logs).KTOTrainer
    SimPO (Meng et al. 2024, arXiv 2405.14734)No reference model; scores each answer by its average per-token log-probability and adds a target margin.Memory is tight (no reference copy) and length bias is a worry.trl.experimental.cpo.CPOConfig(loss_type="simpo", cpo_alpha=0.0)
    ORPO (Hong et al. 2024, arXiv 2403.07691)SFT loss plus an odds-ratio preference term; no reference model.One stage from a base model.trl.experimental.orpo
    Robust DPO (Chowdhury et al. 2024, arXiv 2403.00409)Assumes a fraction of labels are flipped and corrects for it.Noisy preference labels.loss_type=["robust"], label_smoothing=0.1

    Online or iterative DPO is the other direction: sample fresh answers from the current model, label them, and train again, rather than training once on a fixed set of pairs. BrewSLM's recipes cover DPO and ORPO; the other rows are TRL options you would run outside it.

    What to watch while it trains

    DPO's loss alone tells you little. TRL logs four reward metrics every step, where each "reward" is β × (policy log-prob − reference log-prob) for that answer:

    • rewards/chosen and rewards/rejected: how far the policy has moved each answer relative to the reference.
    • rewards/margins: chosen minus rejected. It should grow, then level off.
    • rewards/accuracies: the share of pairs where the chosen reward beats the rejected one, on the training batch.
    import torch
from datasets import Dataset
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
from peft import LoraConfig
from trl import DPOConfig, DPOTrainer

model_id = "HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct"   # start from your SFT checkpoint
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
dtype = torch.bfloat16 if torch.cuda.is_available() else torch.float32
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=dtype)

pairs = Dataset.from_list([   # conversational prompt / chosen / rejected rows
    {"prompt":   [{"role": "user", "content": "Why is the sky blue? Answer for a five-year-old."}],
     "chosen":   [{"role": "assistant", "content": "Sunlight has many colours, and the air bounces the blue around the most."}],
     "rejected": [{"role": "assistant", "content": "Rayleigh scattering scales with the inverse fourth power of wavelength."}]},
] * 8)                        # a smoke test; real runs use hundreds to thousands of distinct pairs

args = DPOConfig(
    output_dir="dpo-out",
    beta=0.1,                    # KL anchor: higher = closer to the reference
    loss_type=["sigmoid"],       # plain DPO; "ipo", "robust", ... are other rows of the table
    learning_rate=1e-5,
    per_device_train_batch_size=4,
    bf16=torch.cuda.is_available(),   # set by hardware; CPU runs in fp32
    max_steps=2, logging_steps=1, report_to="none",
)
trainer = DPOTrainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=pairs, processing_class=tok,
                     peft_config=LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, target_modules="all-linear",
                                            task_type="CAUSAL_LM"))
trainer.train()
for row in trainer.state.log_history:
    if "rewards/margins" in row:
        print({k: round(v, 4) for k, v in row.items() if k.startswith("rewards/")})
# step 1: all zeros (policy == reference, loss = ln 2 = 0.693)
# step 2: chosen > 0, rejected < 0, margin > 0

    At step 1 every reward is 0, because the LoRA policy still equals the reference, and the loss is ln 2 ≈ 0.693. What healthy looks like after that:

    • The margin rises and then flattens, and accuracy climbs well above 0.5 and stays below 1.0 on held-out pairs. Training accuracy pinned at 1.0 early, with the margin still racing upward, usually means the pairs are too easy or the run is over-optimizing: raise β or stop sooner.
    • Watch rewards/chosen on its own. If it goes negative while the margin grows, the model is pushing both answers down and the rejected one faster. That is the next failure mode.
    • Log the same metrics on an eval split of pairs (eval_dataset); a training margin that keeps growing while the eval margin falls is overfitting, as in SFT.

    Failure modes to expect

    • Likelihood displacement. DPO can lower the probability of the chosen answer, as long as the rejected one falls faster, and move that probability mass to answers you never saw, sometimes ones that mean the opposite (Razin et al. 2024, arXiv 2410.08847). Symptom: rewards/chosen going negative. Mitigations: a higher β, fewer steps, pairs whose chosen and rejected answers differ clearly, or an SFT term on the chosen answers (TRL can combine loss_type=["sigmoid", "sft"]).
    • Verbosity exploitation. If chosen answers tend to be longer, DPO learns "longer wins" and output length creeps up (Park et al. 2024, arXiv 2403.19159). Check the length distribution of chosen vs rejected before training, and track mean output length after it.
    • Off-policy pairs. Pairs written by some other model teach less than pairs sampled from your own SFT model, because they rank answers your model would never produce (Tajwar et al. 2024, arXiv 2404.14367). Where you can, sample two answers from your SFT model and have a reviewer or a judge pick one.
    • Noisy labels. Judges and annotators disagree. Keep only pairs where the judge gives the same verdict with the answers in both orders, and consider Robust DPO's label smoothing.

    On the platform

    Both are scored by the AlignmentHandler (Track 3's evaluation dispatcher). Its metric is a similarity proxy: the token-F1 of the model's output against chosen and against rejected. A row counts as preference-correct when the output is closer to chosen, and the mean gap is reported as the alignment margin. That is not DPO's reward margin (the β-scaled log-probability gap), which BrewSLM does not compute today, so treat the number as a rough signal. And preflight will block a DPO run if the preference-training dependency is missing — a typed blocker, not a mid-run crash.

    When to reach for preference tuning

    • Use SFT when there's a correct answer (classification, extraction, format).
    • Add DPO/ORPO when "better" is a judgment: tone, helpfulness, refusing badly, verbosity, style.
    • Prefer ORPO for a simpler one-stage pipeline from a base model; DPO when you already have a solid SFT checkpoint to align.
    • Prefer KTO when your feedback is single thumbs-up / thumbs-down, not pairs.

    Did it help? Evaluating a preference-tuned model

    There is no single right answer to score against, so compare the tuned model with the SFT model it started from:

    • Pairwise win rate. For each held-out prompt, show a judge (a person or an LLM judge, Lesson 2.16) both models' answers and ask which is better. Ask twice with the order swapped and count a win only when both verdicts agree; LLM judges are known to favour one position (Zheng et al. 2023, arXiv 2306.05685).
    • Control for length. Report mean output length next to the win rate. A win rate that rises only because answers got longer is the verbosity failure above, not a better model.
    • Held-out preference accuracy. On held-out pairs, the share where the tuned model's reward for the chosen answer beats the rejected one (TRL's rewards/accuracies on an eval_dataset). Cheap, and no judge needed.
    • Check the task did not regress. Re-run the SFT model's own eval; preference tuning can cost task accuracy.

    Key idea

    Preference tuning optimizes chosen over rejected, not a single right answer. DPO does this directly (no reward model) against a frozen reference, with beta setting how tightly it is held there (higher β = smaller moves); ORPO folds preference into the SFT loss for a one-stage run; IPO, KTO and SimPO change the loss, the data shape or drop the reference. Watch rewards/chosen as well as the margin, and judge the result with order-swapped, length-aware win rates. Reach for them when 'better' is a judgment, not a label.

    Key terms

    preference data
    (prompt, chosen, rejected) triples: two responses with one marked better.
    DPO
    Direct Preference Optimization — derives a loss from preference pairs directly, no separate reward model.
    reference model
    A frozen copy of the starting model DPO anchors to, so the policy doesn't drift arbitrarily.
    beta
    The strength of DPO's KL anchor to the reference model: higher β keeps the policy closer to the reference, lower β lets it move further. (In BrewSLM's ORPO recipe the same key is ORPO's λ.)
    ORPO
    Odds Ratio Preference Optimization — adds a preference term to the SFT loss for single-stage alignment, no reference model.
    DPO family
    Offline preference losses that build on DPO: IPO (bounded margin), KTO (unpaired good/bad labels), SimPO (no reference model), ORPO (SFT plus odds ratio), Robust DPO (noisy labels).
    rewards/margins
    TRL's logged mean gap between the chosen and rejected rewards, each β × (policy − reference log-probability). It should rise, then level off.
    likelihood displacement
    DPO lowering the chosen answer's probability while widening the margin, shifting mass to unseen answers (arXiv 2410.08847).
    AlignmentHandler
    The BrewSLM evaluation handler for DPO/ORPO models; scores outputs by token-F1 similarity to chosen vs rejected (a proxy, not the DPO reward margin).
